Data protection and security

Source: vignettes/articles/data-protection.Rmd
data-protection.Rmd

SRTR standard analysis files (SAFs) are restricted data. This page says what sRtr does to help keep them protected, what it does not do, and what is planned. It is a first version: sRtr’s protections are still being built, and each one is added here when it arrives. Planned items link to their GitHub issue, where the design is discussed.

Nothing here replaces your data use agreement (DUA) or your data security plan. They decide what you may do; sRtr can only make the safe path easier.

Your agreement sets the rules

SRTR releases SAFs only under a signed DUA, and every request that needs a DUA must also have a data security plan and a research plan (SRTR 2026). Those documents decide where the files may be stored, who may see them, and what may be reported from them. sRtr cannot check any of this.

SRTR’s public pages state no rule on the smallest count you may report. The signed DUA is not public, so read yours for a reporting clause. For data linked to Medicare records, the CMS cell size suppression policy applies: no count from 1 to 10, and no number from which such a count can be worked out (CMS 2020). For SRTR data alone, masking counts below 11 is common practice rather than a published SRTR rule. sRtr’s articles follow it.

Nothing on this page is legal advice. A protection marked “in place” lowers a risk; it does not show that an analysis meets your agreement.

Where sRtr reads and writes

  • Reading. load_srtr_file() reads SAFs only from the folder you set with set_srtr_wd() (the SRTR_WD environment variable), on your own computer.
  • The network. sRtr sends nothing from your files anywhere. Only two functions use the network, and both download public map layers from HRSA without sending anything about your data: get_hrsa_transplant_centers() and get_hrsa_opo_service_areas(). The Coverage gain article also downloads public Census data, with your own API key.
  • Writing. sRtr’s functions write nothing outside R’s temporary folder (tempdir()) unless you give them a path. One function writes outside it when you ask: set_srtr_wd(path, permanent = TRUE) saves the folder’s path, not any data, to your ~/.Renviron file.

Keep the SAF folder where your security plan says. In particular, keep it out of any folder tracked by git, and out of folders that a cloud service synchronizes, unless your plan covers that service.

Planned: set_srtr_wd() will warn when the folder is inside a git repository and not ignored (#294).

Keep SAFs out of version control

A SAF, or any file made from one, that is committed to git is copied to every clone and stays in the history after it is deleted. Pushing it to a private repository is still a disclosure.

sRtr’s own repository has two guards. Its .gitignore file keeps SAF formats out of commits, and a check on GitHub fails on SAF formats, on text files whose headers have SRTR identifier columns, and on files over 5 MB. You can add the same patterns to the .gitignore of your own analysis project:

# SRTR data: never commit
*.[sS][aA][sS]7[bB][dD][aA][tT]
*.[sS][aA][sS]7[bB][cC][aA][tT]
*.[xX][pP][tT]
*.[pP][aA][rR][qQ][uU][eE][tT]
*.[fF][eE][aA][tT][hH][eE][rR]
*.[aA][rR][rR][oO][wW]
*.[dD][tT][aA]
*.[sS][aA][vV]

These patterns catch the usual file formats only. They do not catch .rds, .RData or .csv files you write from a SAF, and git add -f overrides them. Keep files made from SAFs in the same protected folder as the SAFs, not in the project.

Planned (#294; function names are provisional):

  • a function that scans a project folder for files that look like SRTR data;
  • a check when sRtr is attached, which warns, naming paths only, about such files that git does not ignore (on by default, with an option to turn it off);
  • helpers that add the patterns above to your project’s .gitignore and install a commit hook that runs the scan on staged files.

Share results, not records

Share aggregate results only, never rows. Mask any count from 1 to 10, and do not share a total beside masked parts, or two counts that differ by a little, because a reader can work out the small count by subtraction. Checking sRtr on your own SAFs explains each rule with code.

Planned: a function that checks tables, model output and figures for small cells, with the threshold set by an option (#295), and small-cell flags in sRtr’s summary functions (#11).

AI assistants and help requests

A chat with an AI assistant, a GitHub issue, a forum post and an email to a colleague outside your agreement are all disclosures. When you ask for help:

  • share your code, column names and masked counts;
  • do not paste rows, printed data frames, or the output of head(), str() or View() on SAF data, and do not attach files made from SAFs;
  • treat sRtr’s error and warning messages, and test failures, as output from your files: they can include exact counts, and some quote values from a column (for example, codes that no format lists). Before you share one, replace every count, value and identifier it contains, or reproduce the message on a few made-up rows and share that instead.

An assistant that can read your files or run commands on your computer can read the SAF folder too. Do not give it access to that folder unless your security plan covers the tool.

Contributing without SRTR data

sRtr is developed without SRTR data. Its tests run on small, made-up data; the tests that need real SAFs skip unless SRTR_LIVE_TESTS and SRTR_WD are set, and are run only by people whose own DUA covers the files, on their own computers. Results from those runs are shared as masked aggregate counts. Development and how to contribute lists work that needs no SAFs.

Planned: a contributor guide to keeping SRTR data out of the repository (#94), a synthetic SAF generator for tests and examples (#1), and public center-level tables for examples that need no DUA (#13).

What sRtr does not do

  • sRtr is not a secure computing environment. It does not encrypt files, control who can open them or keep an audit log; your institution’s environment provides those.
  • Its checks, now and planned, look for common patterns. A clean check does not show that a folder or a repository holds no patient data.
  • It does not decide what your DUA allows.
